text: A lot of interesting things are happening with the graphics card market. Intel is only releasing models in the low-end(200-300€) range. AMD will release models in the mid-range (€500), with the expected RX 8800/XT model competing with the RTX 4080. Nvidia will probably only release models in the high-end (€800-1000-1500) RTX 5080/90. Everything seems too tuned to me, or at least it will be so at first. The most interesting thing will happen when these three players start entering their comfort zones, and this will not happen before mid-2025. For example, I will be interested in how the Radeon RX 8600 would look compared to the Intel B580. I am interested in how the RTX 5060/Ti would look, I am interested in how the Intel B780/70/50 would look. Right now, things seem like there is something for everyone. Things in Bulgaria, and in Europe in general, are not so good, because the Intel B580 starts at a price of 320-330€, and at this price I think there are better offers, especially on second-hand models. Personally, if I had to buy, I would wait for AMD and Nvidia to release their new models, this will probably lower the prices of their current models.

Sad part is that the Intel part probably won't take the market share from Nvidia, it's going to come from AMD. So either AMD's next generation is going to have to step the game up significantly, which they need to do regardless of Intel's release, and they are going to have to get much more competitive with their prices as a general rule. Also, if Intel sticks with this release and continues to improve the performance of their card after it is in the wild, I'm anticipating that their numbers are going to continue to improve while the 4060, 3060, 7600XT, 6700XT are all running on matured drivers. This could continue to give them a little bit more of an edge as time progresses. 

Would love to see Nvidia lose some of it's market share. However losing it on the bottom end would not effect their top end that is in dire need of reset. But losing some market share might slightly change their pricing strategy of, "i can't believe they will sill buy it at this price, I can't believe their paying, TO THE MOON!!!". AMD's strategy of, "They are paying X the Nvidia cards, so they will pay X price for ours, we don't need to compete on price, just follow the leader". Both companies will blame inflation, AI and any other excuse they can come up with, but apparently, Intel just proved them wrong.  

Also still very much hoping to see a B7XX and B9XX series come out with similar price/performance. Those cards would be an absolute dominator in the current market and absolutely would get my sale. As it is, I'm already on the hunt for a B580 for my son's computer as Intel delivered on it's promises, shows signs of continued support and I really want to encourage this type of business practice. If they continue this trajectory without matching the pricing strategy of AMD and Nvidia, they could see themselves taking over the low end of the GPU market. Kudos to Intel for once not inflating the numbers out of the ballpark of reality, setting a price that doesn't choke a horse, and delivering a good product to market on their second generation!

text:
At 1440p, it's absolutely curb stomping the 4060 8G for 10-15% less if you get the B580 for $250. Obviously, there are a few exceptions, but Intel has actually been supporting these GPUs well with good driver releases. While this is bad for Nvidia, it's worse for AMD, as AMD's entire argument has been value. Intel is providing superior value for the price. The 7600 is anemic at $250, and the the 7600XT is comparable, but the cost per frame is still better for the B580. 

It even compares well to AMD power-wise, with similar frames per watt. No surprise they still trail Nvidia in power efficiency, but a single generation improvement has been massive.

Lastly, we also need to consider that XESS is better than FSR 2/3. I find it produces considerably less artifacts, and a nicer image overall. Both are platform-agnostic, so you can switch them as needed.

I can't believe I'm actually likely to recommend an Intel card. It's really looking good for budget gaming.

text:
Just doing some napkin calculations a hypothetical B770 with 28 cores at a clock speed of 3180 could beat the 4070 in raster and maybe match the 4060ti in RT at 1440p.  They could charge 375 for it.

An 8 core increase corresponds to a 2 render slice increase, which is the increase from an A580 to an A770.  The clock speed difference between those cards was 23.5%, so a 19% increase seems doable.  The price difference between the B580 and B570 is 30, which corresponds to 15 per core, so if they went up 8 cores that would put the price at 370.

Of course this all assumes linearity, which is unlikely to hold, but it might not be that far off.  I tried to account for that by finding a number for the clock speed that would kick the 4070's ass and match the 4060ti at RT, then added 5 to the price.

At least that is my hope because I want to buy one of these to play with. I would also disagree with your stance on using RT under the $600 threshold. RT shadows or contact shadows or even low end RT lighting can increase the feeling of immersion in a game at slightly lower graphical settings on a card like the 6700XT and probably on the B580. You're running these cards at max settings basically and then turning RT on. Why not drop it from ultra to high and turn on RT shadows or lighting and get a taste of both worlds? Blanketly saying that RT is out of the picture for these cards seems a little irresponsible. Great video though and I do still value/respect your opinions. We just don't share the same thoughts about RT. That being said, turning RT off, cranking up the rasterization settings, and getting more frames is always going to be the decision I would make over turning any RT on in the first place.

text:
@thomaszachariadis634  They couldn't feasibly do a 16GB version. The vram capacity configuration options become very limited once you've made the GPU die. As I understand it, they typically can only choose to double vram capacity, or not, on the same GPU. 

With GDDR7 chips, there will eventually be 3GB chips available which can be used instead of 2GB chips, so in that case, adding 50% more vram capacity without changing anything else will be possible, but GDDR7 is probably way too expensive to use with the B580, at least for a model intended to be sold for gaming systems, especially 3GB chips, which would mean that the B580 would go up to 18GB, and they wouldn't be able to make an 18GB version until much later this year anyway. I don't actually know if the B580 would be compatible with GDDR7, but I'm guessing it would be. It's possible we'll see an 18GB version with GDDR7 sold in limited quantities as a workstation graphics card, but there will never be one sold at a competitive price for gaming.

text:
They are priced appropriately, but Intel is surely selling these GPUs at a loss, so they can't afford to actually sell that many of them. Don't get your hopes up. 

The GPU is only about 10% smaller than the one used in the RTX 4070, and is made using the same process node, and the memory configuration is very similar as well, so these likely cost close to the same price as the RTX 4070 to make.

The RTX 4070 is about 45% faster, but likely costs 10% more to make at most, so Intel is WAYYYYY behind still. If these cards aren't normally available for these prices, then it's not that impressive, but I do expect AMD to offer something relatively similar, or at least very competitive with the B580 (but perhaps something faster for 300 or 350 rather than a 250 dollar 12GB card).

text:
I had pretty low expectations, but the value seems hard to argue with. I think the biggest problem I have had with the GPU market is the sub/around 300 segment, where if, lets say you bought a 6600 a couple of years ago for 230, well, all you can buy now is the same card but for 200 instead. What if you bought a 6700 XT 2-3 years ago, well, now you can buy if again for like 290 (or could rather) instead of 350, so there is this "RDNA2 toilet" that is just at the bottom that each year gets slightly cheaper, but from someone who is buying that tier of GPU, there really isn't an upgrade to be had, only a slight discount for what you could have already bought. 

This isn't made better by the fact that last I checked, you can't really buy a 6700 XT anymore, at least at reasonable prices, so there isn't really a card on the market that is designed to compete with this. I always thought that the 7600 in both variants was poor value and agree that the non-xt should be 199 at this point, 6600 is appearing on minimum-spec for Indiana Jones so it is not exactly far off the chopping block of being able to play new games.

With the drivers, you are a madlad so you get CPU/GPU tests up right after a game launches, and it is not uncommon to see the A770/A750 close to bottom of the chart in some recent releases right at launch. And it is both impossible to know how that is going to turn out for B580, and very difficult to set a objective concrete value that you can ascribe to games running perfectly at launch. We will see how next gen GPUs turn out, but I am not really expecting either nVidia or AMD to release a card at $250 MSRP if I am being honest.

text: @carlosmagnomacieira8210  "A" for letters of the alphabet. The newer the alphabet, the latest the generations. So "B" is basically next generations. The first number represents the graphics tier; 3 for lower tier, 5 for mid to upper tier and 7 for top and flagship tiers. The last two are the tiers of tiers. Basically whether it's lower pack or upper pack. 80 is top while 70 is mid. 50 or 30 is probably low to laptop tier.

text:
@syncmonism  Unlikely. PCIe bandwidth only makes a big difference performance when you're close to running out of VRAM, which is much less of a problem for the B580 than it is for the RTX 4060 and RX 7600; which are also PCIe 4.0 x8 cards, but with only 8GB.
You can find PCIe scaling benchmarks which compare the the RX 5500 XT 4GB and 8GB (Hardware Unboxed made a video about this themselves), or which compare the RTX 4060 Ti 8GB and 16GB. The low-capacity versions are often crippled when limited to PCIe 3.0, but the higher-capacity versions normally aren't significantly affected.

TSMC charges around 15'000 per 300mm 5nm wafer. that's gonna make like 200-220 useable dies depending on the yield per wafer, so the silicon alone will be 65-75 ish. 12 gigs of gddr6 is around 40 bucks nowadays. then you need a PCB and a vrm. another 30-40 bucks at least. now add a heatpipe cooler for another 20-ish, assembly, packaging and shipping, and suddenly there's not much room between a 250 bucks msrp and your actual manufacturing costs. and that's before you consider any development costs, the cost of providing drivers, marketing, storage, or anything. 

you can probably get at least 120 more functional 4060 dies out of the same wafer, and you can slap those on cheaper pcbs with cheaper vrms and cheaper coolers.

text:
A few notes about the review: The 12 game average is not an average of ‘raster’ performance, it’s a mix of ray tracing and raster performance. We’re now at a point in time where there are games that exclusively use RT effects, or enable them with higher presets. In this example Star Wars Outlaws is an RT only title and Dragon Age: The Veilguard enables RT with the ‘Ultra’ preset. So the 12 game average is meant to be an overall representation of modern gaming, whereas the RT section is a look at RT performance in games where it really makes a visual difference (based on our testing and opinions).

The review is weighted more on the 12 game average data, which we also use for our value analysis. Moving forward I’m sure we’ll see more games included which use RT effects.
